analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to make, sell, or possess many semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and large-capacity magazines.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 32 cosponsors in November 2017, the bill received one committee hearing and never got a vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess certain semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns, plus any ammunition magazine holding more than 10 rounds. People who already own covered weapons could keep them, but future private sales would require a dealer background check, and those guns would have to be securely stored away from people prohibited from having firearms. The bill lists thousands of hunting and sporting firearms as exempt and lets states use existing anti-crime grant money to run buy-back programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who want a smaller supply of military-style semiautomatic weapons and high-capacity magazines in circulation, and communities affected by mass shootings. Police agencies, nuclear-security workers, and retired officers keep their access through exemptions, and owners of hunting and sporting guns on the exempt list lose nothing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities pushing for gun safety laws

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it a crime to knowingly import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or a large-capacity ammunition feeding device, with exemptions for law enforcement, nuclear-materials security, and retired officers.

People who already own covered weapons may keep them, but future sales or transfers between private parties must go through a licensed dealer with a background check, and grandfathered weapons must be securely stored away from anyone legally barred from having a gun.
Newly manufactured covered weapons and magazines must carry serial numbers and manufacture dates, and the Attorney General must keep and publish a public record of covered weapons used in crimes.
The bill lets state and local governments use existing Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay individuals who turn in covered weapons under a buy-back program.
The bill explicitly exempts a long list of hunting and sporting firearms, including most bolt-action, lever-action, pump, and over-under shotguns and rifles, so those owners are untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and dealers lose the legal market for the covered semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns and for magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Individual owners of grandfathered weapons face new storage duties and a background-check requirement on private sales.

drawbacks.text: The ban is defined by features, not just named models: any semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine plus one listed trait, such as a pistol grip, forward grip, folding stock, barrel shroud, or threaded barrel, counts as a banned assault weapon, a definition critics said captures common firearms that function like many guns on the exempt list.

The bill's stated purpose is 'to ensure that the right to keep and bear arms is not unlimited,' which is the core of the objection from gun-rights supporters who argued the Second Amendment protects ownership of these firearms.

Grandfathering means the millions of covered weapons already in private hands stay legal indefinitely; the bill stops future manufacture and sales but does not remove existing weapons, and the buy-back program it funds is voluntary for states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would cut off future sales of a category of weapons associated with high-profile mass shootings while leaving hunting and sporting firearms untouched and existing owners legal, so its public-safety value depends on how quickly new covered weapons disappear from circulation. The honest cost side: the feature-based definitions are blunt, drawing lines that both sweep in some guns functionally similar to exempt ones and leave similar weapons on the market, and grandfathering blunts the near-term effect. Supporters would argue those compromises are what made the bill acceptable to sport shooters; opponents would say the definitions were still too broad.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got a single hearing in March 2018, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 without a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on November 8, 2017, with 32 cosponsors, all Democrats except one Independent.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The committee held a hearing on March 14, 2018, but took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.
No roll-call vote was ever taken in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers and sellers kept the existing market for semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and high-capacity magazines, and opponents of new gun restrictions kept the status quo without ever having to vote on the bill.

industries.industry: Semiautomatic rifle, pistol, and shotgun manufacturers
industries.note: New manufacture, import, sale, and transfer of the covered weapons and of any magazine over 10 rounds would become federal crimes, ending the legal market for the AR-15, AK, and similar models the bill names. Existing owners keep their guns, so the loss is to future sales, not to property already owned.

Any magazine, drum, or belt holding more than 10 rounds could no longer be made or sold; existing ones could be kept but not transferred. The industry's core product line would be closed to new sales.
Dealers would lose the ability to sell the covered weapons and magazines, though they would gain the background-check business on private transfers of grandfathered guns.

The bill's Appendix A exempts thousands of named bolt-action, lever-action, pump, and over-under hunting and competition guns, so their products stay fully legal while competitors' tactical-style semiautomatics are banned.
